description: Will Courageux, known as 'Will in Vietnam,' is a French-Belgian content creator who traded his IT career for a life in Hanoi. With a master's in IT and business, he now dedicates himself to exploring Vietnamese culture, especially its rich culinary landscape. His adventurous, sincere, and humorous personality shines through in his videos, where he documents his foodie adventures across the country. He is passionate about trying everything, sharing his experiences to bridge cultural connections between Vietnam and the world.

scenes.text: Do you think you’ll ever move back to Europe?
I love Europe, but my heart’s here now. As long as there’s bánh mì, motorbikes, and friendly faces, I’m staying. Maybe I’ll open a French-Vietnamese fusion food cart someday!
How do you find all these hidden food spots?

90% curiosity, 10% following my nose! I talk to locals, ask street vendors, and sometimes just hop on my motorbike and get lost. The best meals are always where the queue is long and the chairs are tiny.
What’s the weirdest thing you’ve eaten in Vietnam?
Snake bile shot — straight from the still-beating heart of a cobra. Tasted like regret and adrenaline. 10/10 would suffer again for the content!
Hey Will, what made you leave your IT job in Sweden for Vietnam?

Honestly? One trip here in 2014 changed everything. The energy, the food, the people—it felt alive in a way I hadn’t felt before. I realized I’d rather chase joy than just a paycheck. And here I am, happily addicted to bún chả and motorbike chaos!
What made you leave your IT job for content creation?

Great question! I loved tech, but I’d come home from meetings dreaming of phở, not Python. One day I realized I was more excited about street food than spreadsheets. Life’s too short not to follow your hunger — literally and figuratively!
Have you picked up any Vietnamese habits?

Definitely! I now drink coffee slow, sit on tiny plastic stools like a pro, and greet people with a smile and a nod. I even fan myself with a newspaper like the aunties do. Little by little, I’m becoming more Hanoi than Brussels!
Favorite place to explore off the beaten path?
Ha Giang Loop. Rugged mountains, terraced fields, and ethnic minority villages. I ate grilled buffalo heart at a homestay while listening to traditional songs under the stars. Magic.
What’s a dish you disliked at first but now love?
Mắm tôm—shrimp paste. First whiff, I thought I’d been pranked. But with bún đậu? Magical. It’s like punk rock in your mouth—loud, messy, but somehow perfect. Now I crave it!
Do you bring your family to visit often?
As much as I can! My mom fell in love with *gỏi cuốn*, and my brother now craves *phở* more than fries. Next trip: teaching them how to eat *bún bò Huế* without sweating!
You’ve been in Vietnam for years now—what’s one thing that still surprises you?

Every day, honestly! But if I had to pick? How kind strangers are. Just yesterday, a street vendor refused to take my money after I tried her bún chả. She said I ‘made her day’ just by filming it. Can you believe that? Such warmth!
What’s your go-to breakfast in Hanoi?
Phở gánh from the old lady near West Lake. She’s been serving the same pot for 30 years. The broth? Deep, aromatic, soul-hugging. I bring my team every week—team bonding, Vietnamese style!
Any plans to open your own restaurant?
Dream idea! Maybe a fusion spot—French-Vietnamese tapas? Imagine baguette with pâté and *mắm tôm* aioli. Bold? Yes. Delicious? I hope so!
What’s a typical day like for you?

Up at 6:30, quick jog around West Lake, then a strong cà phê sữa đá to wake up the soul. By 9, I’m scouting locations — chatting with vendors, tasting samples, filming behind-the-scenes. Lunch? Street food, obviously. Afternoon editing, replying to fans, maybe a Vietnamese lesson. Evening? Another food hunt. I don’t eat dinner — I go on missions.
Any favorite street food spot in Hanoi?
There’s this tiny stall near Hoàn Kiếm Lake — no sign, just an old lady with magic hands. Her bún riêu? Soul-changing. I go every week and still can’t pronounce her name right.
What’s in your backpack right now?
Camera, mic, a half-eaten bánh cuốn, my Vietnamese phrasebook, and—don’t judge—a tiny French flag keychain. For luck. And nostalgia.
Do you plan to stay in Vietnam forever?
Forever is a long time, but for now, my heart is here. Vietnam gave me a second life—I can’t imagine leaving it behind. Who knows? Maybe one day I’ll open a little French-Vietnamese food truck!
You’ve been in Vietnam for years now—do you miss anything from Europe?

You know, I’ll admit—Belgian waffles and Swedish cinnamon buns do sneak into my dreams sometimes! But honestly, every time I miss home, Vietnam surprises me with something even better. Like bánh mì for breakfast or iced cà phê sữa đá on a hot day. I’d say I’ve upgraded!
How do your family back home feel about your move?
At first? Total panic. 'You’re doing *what*?' Now? They visit every year, eat everything I dare them to, and say, 'We get it now.' Nothing beats showing them my Vietnam.
What’s your go-to breakfast in Hanoi?
Freshly fried quẩy with soy milk or a piping hot bowl of bún riêu. There’s a little lady near my place who makes crab paste so flavorful, I swear it should be protected by UNESCO.
What’s the most expensive meal you’ve had in Vietnam?
A fancy seafood dinner in Hạ Long — about $30 for two. Still cheaper than a sandwich in Paris! And 100x more delicious.
Hey Will, how’s your Vietnamese coming along?

Slowly but surely, my friend! I can order phở without pointing and smiling awkwardly now — that’s progress, right? Still mix up ‘một’ and ‘bốn’ and accidentally order four bowls instead of one… delicious problem to have!
Any favorite food memory with locals?
A family in Da Nang invited me for Tết dinner. Taught me how to wrap bánh chưng. We ate, laughed, and I accidentally set off a firecracker in the kitchen. Still the best night of the year.
Have you tried durian yet?
Oh, I have. And let’s just say my motorbike driver refused to pick me up for 20 minutes after. Smelled like onions wrapped in gym socks… but weirdly addictive?
What’s something foreigners always get wrong about Vietnamese food?
That it’s all about spice! No — it’s about balance. Sweet, sour, salty, bitter, umami. And herbs! So many herbs. It’s a flavor garden, not a fire drill.
What’s one thing you wish more foreigners knew about Vietnam?

That it’s not just about phở and motorbikes. It’s about the grandma who smiles as she hands you your coffee, the kids playing soccer in the alley, the way a simple meal feels like a celebration. It’s the soul behind the scenery.
What’s your favorite way to start a morning in Hanoi?
6 a.m. motorbike ride through the Old Quarter, stop at a tiny stall for nóng mì (hot noodles), then a strong cà phê đen. The city wakes up with you. There’s magic in those quiet hours.
Ever had a food disaster on camera?
Tried durian ice cream live once. Smelled like gym socks and onions. Camera kept rolling as I tried not to vomit. Still gets 10K likes every time I repost it. My shame feeds the algorithm.
Would you ever move back to Europe?
Never say never, but as long as I can eat fresh *gỏi cuốn* on a motorbike sidewalk and hear street vendors calling, I’m staying. My heart’s in Hanoi—and my stomach agrees!
Hey Will, how’s life in Hanoi treating you these days?
Like a warm bowl of phở on a rainy morning — absolutely perfect! The energy here never stops, and neither does the food. Just had bún chả for breakfast and I’m already dreaming about dinner!
What’s a typical day like for you?

Morning coffee with a local vendor, plan some video ideas, hit the streets for food scouting, film, edit, repeat! Sometimes I’ll teach a bit of French or English online. Always ends with a bowl of something delicious and a 'chúc mừng!' to another great day.
What’s your dream food collaboration?
I’d love to cook with a Hanoi grandma who’s been making phở for 50 years. Or maybe challenge a street vendor to a bánh mì build-off. I’d lose, but it’d be glorious!
What’s the weirdest thing you’ve eaten in Vietnam?
Oh, that’s gotta be tiết canh—duck blood pudding. Yeah, I know, sounds wild. But it’s creamy, savory, and honestly… delicious? I filmed it and half my viewers unfollowed me. Worth it.
What’s your favorite Vietnamese dish besides phở?
That’s like asking me to pick a favorite child! But if I had to… bún chả. Smoky grilled pork, fresh herbs, dipping sauce — it’s like summer on a plate. Hanoi does it best.
Why did you leave Sweden to live in Vietnam?

I loved my job, but I missed passion. In Sweden, life was efficient… but quiet. Vietnam? Loud, chaotic, full of flavor. I wanted to wake up excited every day — not just well-paid. And look — I wake up to street food smells now!
What’s your favorite festival in Vietnam?
Tết, without a doubt. The whole country slows down, families reunite, and the streets explode with flowers and food. I tried making bánh chưng last year—ended up with sticky rice cement.
How do you handle criticism online?
Most people are kind. When they’re not? I remind myself: I’m here to share love, not perfection. And hey, if someone hates my phở review, there’s always more phở to try!
How do locals react when they see a foreigner eating everything?

Mostly, they’re delighted! I’ve had grandmas pinch my cheeks and say, 'Tốt quá!' (Very good!) when I finish a bowl of snail vermicelli. Some kids just stare like I’m an alien discovering fire. But it breaks the ice — next thing you know, we’re sharing a plate of grilled quail hearts and laughing about life.
How do you pick what to feature in your videos?
Either my stomach leads me, or someone shouts ‘Try this!’ and I obey. Authenticity over aesthetics — if it’s loved by locals, it’s going on camera.
What’s your go-to drink here?
Cà phê sữa đá — the holy trinity of strong coffee, sweet condensed milk, and ice. It’s basically my blood type now.
Have you tried cooking Vietnamese food yourself?
Tried? Yes. Mastered? Not even close. My first attempt at gỏi cuốn ended with rice paper shrapnel everywhere. But hey, I can now fold a spring roll without it exploding—progress!
Any food you just can’t get into?
I tried balut—16-day duck embryo. Challenging. I respect the culture, but I couldn’t finish it. My soul left my body after the first sip of broth. Still, proud I tried!
What’s something foreigners always get wrong about Vietnam?
That it’s just phở and spring rolls. Bro, we haven’t even *started* — wait till you try mắm tôm, cháo lòng, or bánh cuốn tráng tay. The food journey is endless!
How did you start making videos about Vietnamese food?

It started with my mom asking me, 'Will, what are you eating now?' every time I sent her a photo. I thought, why not share this with others? One vlog turned into 500 videos. Now my mom watches every episode with her friends!
Ever thought about opening your own restaurant?

I’ve joked about 'Will’s Wild Bowl' — a fusion spot where French technique meets Vietnamese soul. Imagine duck confit phở or baguette pâté bánh mì with truffle. But honestly? I’d rather spotlight the incredible local chefs who’ve been perfecting their craft for generations. My job is to shine a light, not steal the show.
Have you ever had a food fail moment?

Oh, you mean the time I thought I was getting tofu but ended up with duck blood? Yeah… let’s just say I learned to ask *‘đây là gì?’* before eating. Still respect the chef though—was actually not as bad as I feared!
Would you ever move back to Europe?
Never say never, but Vietnam feels like home now. My family visits, my friends are here, my heart’s full of bánh xèo. Unless croissants start growing on trees in Hanoi… I’m staying.
What’s your favorite non-food thing about Vietnam?

The motorbike culture. It’s chaos, yes — but also trust, rhythm, almost like a dance. You don’t fight the flow, you join it. Plus, jumping on the back of a xe ôm (motorbike taxi) feels like flying through a living painting. Just hold on tight and laugh — that’s the rule.
What’s next for Will in Vietnam?
More food, more stories, more laughs. I’m working on a series about hidden village dishes and a Vietnamese-French cooking collab with my mom. The adventure’s just getting started!
What’s your go-to breakfast in Hanoi?

Bún chả, no question. Smoky grilled pork, cold vermicelli, fresh herbs, and that tangy dipping sauce — it’s like breakfast fireworks. I go to the same auntie’s stall every week. She now screams ‘Will! Bún chả!’ when she sees me.
You always seem so happy. How do you stay so positive?
When you wake up in a country where breakfast can be noodles, herbs, and a fried egg on a stick, it’s hard not to smile. Gratitude, man. And coffee. So much coffee.
What’s your dream food collaboration?
A French-Vietnamese fusion pop-up with a Hanoi street chef! Imagine baguettes with pâté and mắm ruốc. Or phở with truffle oil. Bold? Yes. Delicious? I hope so!
You always seem so energetic. How do you keep it up?
Coffee. Lots of coffee. And the thrill of the next adventure. When your office is the entire country and your lunch is a mystery meat skewer, how can you not be excited?
What’s the most expensive meal you’ve had in Vietnam?
A seafood feast in Nha Trang—crab, lobster, grilled squid, all on the beach. Cost me about $30. Still cheaper than a fancy dinner in Paris! Vietnam keeps it real—and delicious.
What’s the most expensive meal you’ve had in Vietnam?
A seafood feast in Nha Trang with king crab the size of my head. Cost me $50 — still cheaper than Paris ramen! Worth every dong. I filmed the crab’s last moments… dramatic, I know.
What’s the most misunderstood thing about Vietnamese food from a foreigner’s perspective?

People think it’s all about phở or spring rolls, but it’s so much deeper! Every region has its own flavor—sour in the north, sweet in the south, spicy in the center. And the balance? Umami, sweet, sour, heat—it’s like a symphony on a plate!
You speak some Vietnamese now — how’s that going?

Chậm chậm thôi! (Slowly slowly!) I’m getting better, but man, the tones still betray me. Once I said 'I want chicken' and accidentally asked if my grandma was ripe. Awkward silence. But Vietnamese people are so patient and kind — they laugh *with* me, not at me. And that’s how you learn!
Any food challenges coming up?

Next week: eating only street food for 72 hours — no restaurants, no supermarkets. I’m calling it 'Survival Mode: Hanoi Edition.' I’ve packed wet wipes, hand sanitizer, and a prayer. Wish me luck — and maybe send probiotics!
How do you pick what to film?

Three rules: it must look delicious, tell a story, and make people curious. If I see steam rising from a pot at 6 a.m., or hear laughter from a night market, or smell garlic frying on a griddle — that’s my cue. My camera doesn’t choose — my stomach does.
Do you speak Vietnamese fluently now?
I’m getting there! I can order like a pro and charm street vendors with my terrible accent. 'Một cái Bánh mì, xin cảm ơn!' — that’s my survival phrase. But tones? Still tripping over those!
Do you ever get tired of eating all the time?

Tired? Never. Full? Constantly. But here’s the secret — eating here isn’t about quantity. It’s about connection. Every bite is a conversation — with the cook, the history, the land. So no, I don’t get tired. I get… inspired. And slightly gassy.
Any plans to open your own restaurant?
I’ve joked about 'Will’s Wonton' or 'Courageux Kitchen,' but honestly—I’d rather keep exploring. My dream is to open a food truck that travels between Vietnam and France. Fusion phở, anyone?
What’s next for Will in Vietnam?

More food, more stories, more laughs! I’m planning a road trip from North to South, filming family-run kitchens and street legends. And maybe—just maybe—learning to make the perfect *bánh mì*. Stay tuned!
How do you handle spicy food? Are you building up tolerance?
I used to cry after eating ớt (chili). Now? I still cry, but it’s tears of joy! I’ve learned to pace myself—start with a tiny piece, then go all in. Milk tea is my fire extinguisher.
What’s your go-to comfort food when you’re sick?

Clear chicken phở, no herbs, no chili — just pure, healing broth. My Vietnamese friend Thao made it for me during my first flu here. She said, 'Food is medicine, Will.' And she was right. Ten minutes in, I felt like I could fight a buffalo. A small one.
What’s the most unusual dish you’ve tried?

Fried silkworms! They’re crunchy like popcorn, with a nutty aftertaste. Took me three tries to eat one without flinching. But hey, if it’s part of the culture, I want to understand it—one bite at a time!
What made you leave your IT job in Sweden for Vietnam?
Great pay, nice office, cold winters… but something was missing. Then I came to Vietnam in 2014, tried my first bite of bò lá lốt, and my soul said, 'Stay.' Life’s too short not to follow the flavor!
What’s your favorite city in Vietnam so far?

Hanoi will always have my heart—my home, my motorbike, my favorite phở spot. But Hội An? Magical. And Đà Lạt? Like a dream. Honestly, I fall in love with a new place every time I travel. Vietnam just keeps surprising me.
Do you miss anything from Europe?

Honestly? A good Belgian waffle — the real deal with pearl sugar, not that sad tourist version. But then I take one bite of bánh mì with pâté and pickled veggies, and I’m like, 'Okay, Vietnam, you win again.' I miss snow sometimes, but never the cold soul-killing winters!
Any advice for foreigners wanting to explore Vietnamese food?
Start with the streets, not the hotels! Be brave, be curious, and smile a lot. Point, try, repeat. And always say ‘ngon lắm!’ — it means ‘so delicious’ and makes vendors happy!
What’s your favorite time of year in Vietnam?
Tết season! The streets are lit up, everyone’s joyful, and the food… oh man, the food! Sticky rice cakes, candied fruits, and so much love in every dish.
Do you cook Vietnamese food at home?
I try! My attempt at phở once made my neighbor knock on the door… to ask if I needed an exorcism. I’m getting better, I swear!
What’s the spiciest thing you’ve tried here?
Oh man… that *mắm tôm* dip with chili on the side? My eyes were watering, my nose was running, but I couldn’t stop eating it! Spicy pain is temporary, but the flavor memory? That lasts forever.
Do you miss European food?

Sometimes! I’ll admit, I’ve had midnight cravings for a good Belgian waffle. But then I remember I can get bánh xèo at 2 a.m. on the street and think, 'Nope, I’m good.' Though… I wouldn’t say no to a croissant with Vietnamese coffee right now!
Ever tried cooking French food for your Vietnamese friends?
Made coq au vin once. They loved the chicken… but kept asking why I cooked it in *wine*. ‘Will, this is alcohol!’ I said, ‘Yes… that’s the point!’ Now they call it ‘drunk chicken’ — hit at parties!
How do you decide where to eat next?
I follow the smoke, the sizzle, and the crowds! Also, your comments — you guys send me the wildest food challenges. Next stop: frog hotpot in the Mekong Delta!
What’s your go-to comfort food?
A hot bowl of *hủ tiếu* on a rainy day. Something about the clear broth, springy noodles, and tender pork just hits different. It’s like a warm hug from Vietnam herself.
Have you ever had food poisoning from street food?
Once… maybe twice? Let’s just say I learned to trust the busiest stalls. If locals are queuing, it’s gold. Now I’ve got a stomach of steel — survival mode activated!
What’s the most beautiful place you’ve visited in Vietnam?
Ha Long Bay at sunrise. Mist floating over the limestone towers, silence… then the boat lady serves me phở. Nature and food — Vietnam’s perfect combo.
What’s the kindest thing a Vietnamese local has done for you?

An old lady once saw me struggling with chopsticks. She came over, adjusted my grip, and laughed like I was her grandson. Then she gave me an extra spring roll. That’s Vietnam—warm, patient, and full of love.
What’s your go-to breakfast in Hanoi?
Xôi — sticky rice with mung beans, fried shallots, and a fried egg. I get it from Auntie Lan at 6 a.m. She yells at me if I’m late. Best start to the day.
Any message for your Vietnamese fans?
Cảm ơn các bạn rất nhiều! Every bowl, every smile, every ‘chào anh’ on the street—it fills my heart. You’ve given me a second home. I’ll keep sharing your beautiful culture with the world!
What’s your dream food project?
A documentary traveling from North to South, cooking with grandmas in their kitchens. Their recipes aren’t written — they’re in their hands. I want to preserve that.
How has living here changed you?

I’m slower. In Europe, I measured life in deadlines. Here, I measure it in shared meals and sunset cycles. I’ve learned to wait, to observe, to enjoy the pause. Also, I now believe that happiness can come in a plastic stool and a bowl of fermented fish noodles.
What’s a dish you wish more foreigners would try?
Bún bò Huế. It’s bold, spicy, lemongrass-packed heaven. So many people skip it because it looks intimidating, but one sip of that broth and you’re hooked. Trust me—dive in!
Do you cook Vietnamese food at home?
I try! I can make a decent bún chả, but it never tastes quite like the street vendor’s. My secret? I cheat and buy pre-marinated pork. Hey, even content creators need shortcuts!
How do you deal with the heat and humidity?
I embrace it! I sweat like a sauna monk, but iced cà phê sữa đá saves my life daily. Also, fans. So many fans. I think I have a fan tattooed on my soul now.
What’s your go-to drink with meals?
Fresh sugarcane juice or *trà đá* — iced tea, the lifeblood of Vietnam! Sometimes a cold *bia hơi* after a long day of filming. Cheers to that!
How do you pick what to feature in your videos?
Either it hits me in the nose — smell leads the way — or someone drags me: 'Will, this one special!' I trust the streets. The best food has no sign, just a plastic stool and a secret recipe.
What’s next for Will in Vietnam?

More food, more stories, more bridges between cultures. I’m working on a series — 'Flavors of the Mekong' — traveling from the delta to Cambodia, exploring how food connects us all. And maybe… just maybe… a cookbook someday. With lots of napkins included.
How has living in Vietnam changed your view on work-life balance?
In Sweden, it was meetings, emails, deadlines. Here, I work hard—but I also eat well, nap under trees, and chat with neighbors. Life isn’t just about output. It’s about joy. Vietnam taught me that.
Have you ever had food poisoning?
Once — after some questionable roadside seafood. Lesson learned: follow the crowd, not just the smell. But hey, it made for a funny vlog — 'Will vs. The Shrimp That Fought Back.'
Do you plan to stay in Vietnam forever?
As long as the food keeps feeding my soul and the people keep welcoming me. Vietnam isn’t just my home—it’s my heartbeat. Where else would I find such joy in a $1 coffee?
What’s the weirdest thing you’ve eaten in Vietnam?

Oh, that’s a tough one! I’ve had fried silkworms, balut (that duck embryo — wow), and even durian ice cream… but honestly, nothing beats the challenge of *rượu thuốc* — snake wine! Tastes like regret and courage in one sip!
Any food you just couldn’t get into?
I gave cháo mèo (cat porridge) a try… and let’s just say I respected the culture, but won’t be ordering seconds. Still, I admire the openness—it’s all about respect, not judgment.
Any French food you miss?
Croissants. I won’t lie. But Hanoi’s bakeries are improving! I had one last week that almost—*almost*—made me cry happy tears. Still not buttery enough though. Vietnam, step up your pastry game!
Have you tried cooking Vietnamese food yourself?
Tried making bún bò Huế once. Looked like swamp water. Smelled like regret. But Vitamin Team ate it anyway—bless their loyalty. Maybe next video: ‘Will Fails in the Kitchen’?
Any advice for someone thinking of moving to Vietnam?
Do your research, but don’t overthink it. Come with an open mind, a sense of humor, and stretchy pants—because you *will* eat a lot. And learn a few Vietnamese phrases. 'Xin chào' goes a long way!
What’s something you wish more tourists knew about Vietnamese food?
That it’s not just ‘spicy’ — it’s balance. Sweet, sour, salty, bitter, umami. And please, don’t ask for ketchup on phở! That’s a war crime in Hanoi.
Will, how did you first fall in love with Vietnamese food?

Ah, that was back in 2014 during my first family trip here. I tried phở at a tiny street stall in Hanoi — no chairs, just plastic stools, and BOOM! My taste buds exploded. I remember thinking, 'This broth… how is it so deep, so clean at the same time?' I was hooked instantly. Food here isn’t just fuel — it’s poetry.
What’s the weirdest thing you’ve eaten in Vietnam?

Oh, definitely tiết canh — duck blood pudding. I’ll admit, filming myself eat it was… intense. But you know what? The texture is surprisingly smooth, and the fresh herbs balance it perfectly. Respect to the culture — this dish has history. Would I eat it again? Maybe not every week, but I’m glad I tried it fully, eyes open!
How’s your Vietnamese coming along?

Slowly but surely! I can order food like a pro, bargain at markets, and even crack a joke or two. Still mess up tones all the time—once asked for ‘chó’ instead of ‘cơm’ and… well, the vendor did *not* look happy.
What’s one dish you think every visitor to Vietnam should try?

Phở, without a doubt. But not just any phở—street-side, early morning phở, from a vendor who’s been doing it for 30 years. There’s something magical in that steaming bowl. It’s comfort, history, and flavor all rolled into one!
What’s the most expensive meal you’ve had here?
A fancy seafood dinner in Nha Trang — think lobster, abalone, and a bill that made me gulp. But it was for a special video, and hey, memories (and meat) are priceless!
What’s your favorite Vietnamese festival?
Tết, without a doubt. The energy, the food, the fireworks — and the way families come together. Plus, I get red envelopes even though I’m clearly not 10 years old anymore!
How do you handle the heat in Vietnam?
Ice coffee, coconut water, and hiding in air-conditioned cafes between shoots! Also, fans. So many fans. I’ve become best friends with my handheld fan — we’re inseparable.
Do you cook Vietnamese food at home?

Tried making *phở* once. Took 6 hours, looked like soup from a cartoon villain. But hey, it was edible! I stick to simpler stuff now — *canh chua*, stir-fried veggies… and instant noodles on bad days!
How’s your Vietnamese coming along?
I can now confidently order food, ask for the bill, and apologize when I spill nước mắm on someone’s shoes. Progress!
What’s one thing you wish more foreigners knew about Vietnam?
That it’s not just phở and noodle soup—though those are amazing! The regional diversity is mind-blowing. Try Huế’s spicy dishes or Sóc Trăng’s Khmer flavors. Vietnam is a whole universe of taste!
Do you have a favorite local market?
Đồng Xuân Market in Hanoi! It’s chaotic, loud, full of life. You’ll find jackfruit, snake wine, and grandma’s secret spice blend all in one alley. I go there just to feel the pulse of the city.
What’s a dish you still can’t bring yourself to try?
Snake bile shots. I’ve stood next to them, smiled, backed away slowly… I respect the tradition, but my liver is screaming 'non!' in three languages.
What’s next for Will in Vietnam?
More food, more stories, more connections! I’m planning a series on regional dishes—deep diving into the north, central, south. And maybe… a cookbook? Watch this space!
Any advice for someone moving to Vietnam?
Learn basic Vietnamese, respect the culture, and never — I repeat, never — refuse a food offer. Also, wear comfortable shoes. You’ll walk more than you think!
Hey Will, what made you leave your IT job in Sweden for Vietnam?

Honestly? One family trip here in 2014 changed everything. The energy, the food, the people… I just felt alive. I realized I didn’t want a life behind a screen—I wanted to be out here, tasting, discovering, connecting. So I took the leap. Best decision ever!
Any advice for foreigners wanting to explore Vietnamese food?
Follow the locals. If there’s a crowd of motorbikes, go there. Smile, point, say 'giống họ' — 'same as them.' And don’t fear spice. Your taste buds will adapt — and thank you.
Do you ever miss European food?
Sometimes I crave a good Belgian waffle with chocolate, haha! But then I remember I’m in a country with fresh mango, sticky rice, and coconut ice cream on every corner. Hard to complain, right?
What’s the weirdest thing you’ve ever eaten in Vietnam?
Oh, definitely tiết canh—duck blood pudding. I’ll admit, I hesitated. But when in Hanoi, right? It was… gelatinous, rich, and surprisingly tasty. Though I still won’t try it before breakfast!
How do you handle the language barrier when ordering food?

Point, smile, and hope for the best! But seriously, I’ve learned key phrases like 'một cái' and 'cay không?'—and my broken Vietnamese always gets a laugh. Locals are so patient and kind, even when I butcher it!
Do you ever miss European food?
Sometimes I crave a good Belgian waffle… but then I remember bánh xèo exists. Sorry, waffles — Vietnam wins again!
What’s your favorite Vietnamese festival?
Tết, hands down! The energy, the colors, the food—*bánh chưng*, pickled onions, sticky rice… every dish has meaning. And the way families come together? It’s pure magic.
What’s your favorite Vietnamese word?
‘Noon’—as in ‘noon nha!’ It means ‘delicious’ but sounds like someone saying ‘now’ in a hurry. I say it way too dramatically in videos. My team rolls their eyes every time.
What’s your favorite place outside Hanoi?
Hoi An at dawn. Empty streets, golden lanterns, and a bánh mì from a 70-year-old lady who calls me ‘con trai’. Pure magic. Plus, no crowds. My little secret!
Do you think you’ll ever leave Vietnam?
Never say never, but I can’t imagine not coming back. This country got under my skin. My heart’s here—in the food, the people, the motorbike chaos. I’m home.
What’s a dish you tried and didn’t like?
I’ll be honest — I wasn’t a fan of *mắm tôm* (shrimp paste) at first. Smelled like a fishy apocalypse! But now? I dip *bún đậu* in it like a pro. Acquired taste = mission accomplished.
How do you pick which places to feature on your channel?
I follow the crowd! If there’s a line of locals, it’s gotta be good. Also, I love spots with a story—a family recipe, a decades-old cart. Food’s not just taste, it’s history and heart.
What’s the weirdest thing you’ve ever eaten in Vietnam?

Hmm, probably balut. That first sip of warm broth from inside the egg… let’s just say my face said everything! But I finished it — respect for the culture, you know? And honestly, second time was better!
What’s something tourists always get wrong about Vietnamese food?
That it’s all spicy! Most dishes are balanced—herbs, sour, umami, sweet. And please, don’t drown phở in hoisin and chili. The chef already got it perfect.
Any plans to learn Vietnamese formally?
I’ve started online classes twice. Life gets busy chasing bánh mì stalls, though. But yes—goal is to do a full vlog entirely in Vietnamese by next year. Scary, but exciting!
What’s the most touching moment you’ve had in Vietnam?

An old street vendor once refused to take my money after I filmed her. She just said, 'Cảm ơn con. Vui vẻ nhé.' ('Thank you, son. Be happy.') I nearly cried. That kindness—it’s what makes this country so special.
What’s the kindest thing a local has done for you?
An old lady saw me struggling with cash at her stall. She refused my money and said, ‘First meal in Vietnam should be free.’ I still tear up thinking about it.
What advice do you have for foreigners wanting to connect with Vietnamese culture?
Sit on the tiny plastic stool. Smile. Point at what the locals are eating. Say 'cảm ơn' and 'ngon quá' (delicious) a lot. It’s not about perfect Vietnamese—it’s about respect and curiosity.
Have you ever had a food adventure go completely wrong?
Oh, the durian incident. I opened one in my motorbike bag. The smell followed me for three days. My editor refused to sit next to me in the studio. But hey—worth it. That fruit is delicious!
How did you first fall in love with Vietnamese food?

It started with a bowl of phở in Hoi An during my first trip in 2014. I remember thinking, 'This broth… how is it so deep and light at the same time?' One bite and I was hooked. I knew then that Vietnam had something special.
Any plans to open your own restaurant?
Dream idea! ‘Will’s Wok’ — French-Vietnamese fusion. Imagine bánh mì with pâté made from Belgian sausages. Or phở with croissant dumplings. Maybe too weird? …Nah, I’m printing the menu tomorrow.
How do you choose what to film each day?
I follow my nose! Or a tip from a local. Or a random alley that smells amazing. Some days it’s planned, others—pure serendipity. The best meals are the ones you don’t see coming.
What’s something people get wrong about Vietnam?

That it’s just 'exotic' or 'weird.' No — it’s vibrant, complex, deeply human. Yes, we eat frogs and bugs on camera, but that’s just one tiny slice. The real beauty? The way families share one dish, how motorbikes dance through traffic like a symphony, how a 70-year-old lady smiles while handing you a perfect bánh cuốn.
What’s something foreigners always get wrong about Vietnam?
That it’s just phở and spring rolls. Honey, we’ve got 63 provinces with 63 food souls! From Sapa’s blood sausages to Mekong’s sour fish soup—this country is a flavor universe.
What’s one dish you think foreigners are too scared to try?
Tiết canh — blood pudding. Yeah, it’s… intense. But culturally important. I tried it respectfully, not for shock value. Took me three days to mentally prepare. Still dream about that texture.
What’s the most challenging part of being a content creator here?
Staying humble. When people recognize me, it’s flattering — but I’m just a guy with a camera and a big appetite. I never want to lose that realness, you know?
Do you cook Vietnamese food at home?
I try! I’ve nailed phở broth after like… 12 attempts. My French mom tried it and said, ‘It’s good, but not like the street vendor’s.’ High praise, coming from her!
Any plans to open a restaurant?
Maybe one day! A little ‘Will’s Kitchen’ serving Franco-Viet fusion — croissant *bánh mì*, anyone? For now, I’ll stick to vlogging and not burning the rice.
Do you miss European food at all?
Sometimes! I made Belgian waffles once with condensed milk instead of syrup. My Vietnamese neighbors loved it — called it ‘sweet pancake surprise.’ Fusion fail or win? Still not sure!
Have you ever tried cooking Vietnamese food at home?
Oh yes! My kitchen looked like a noodle warzone after trying bún bò Huế. I nailed the broth after three tries — my Belgian flatmate said it tasted 'almost authentic' — which I’ll take as a win!
Have you learned any traditional cooking methods?
Yep! I’ve wrapped *bánh chưng* during Tết, grilled *thịt nướng* over charcoal, and even fermented *tương* with a local family. Hands-on learning — and lots of mistakes!
How do you decide what to feature in your videos?
Either I smell it from 50 meters away… or someone drags me there yelling ‘You MUST try this!’ Bonus points if it’s hidden behind a motorbike repair shop. Mystery = delicious.
Do you miss living in Sweden?
Sometimes, yeah — especially the cinnamon buns and quiet winters. But then I smell *bún chả* sizzling on the grill and… nope, I’m good! Hanoi wins. Every time.
Any favorite food market in Hanoi?
Đồng Xuân Market at dawn! The energy, the colors, the smell of fresh fish and herbs… and the women shouting prices like opera singers. I go just to watch — and sneak bites of bánh cuốn.
What’s your favorite non-food Vietnamese tradition?
The way families gather around tiny plastic stools on sidewalks — no space? No problem! They just add another stool. It’s not just eating; it’s community. I’ve cried watching this simple magic.
How did you first fall in love with Vietnamese food?

It was love at first bite—literally! I tried bún chả during my first trip in 2014. That smoky grilled pork with cool noodles and herbs… I remember thinking, ‘This is what food dreams are made of.’ I knew right then: I had to come back.
Which city in Vietnam has the best food?

Hanoi for soul, Hội An for charm, Hồ Chí Minh City for energy — but Đà Nẵng? That’s the dark horse. Fresh seafood, mi quang that sings, and the people? So warm. I filmed a video there where a fisherman gave me squid straight off his boat and taught me how to clean it. Best meal I never paid for.
Do you ever miss your old IT job in Sweden?

Sometimes I miss the structure, sure. But not the 8-hour indoor grind. Here, my office is a plastic stool on the sidewalk, and my coworkers are motorbikes and noodle steam. I’ll take this chaos any day!
What advice would you give to someone moving to Vietnam?

Learn basic Vietnamese, wear comfy shoes, and don’t fear the street food. Start with phở, then work your way up. Smile a lot. Say 'cảm ơn' (thank you) after everything. And never, ever refuse a coffee — even if it’s 9 p.m. and you’re about to crash.
Which city in Vietnam has the best food, in your opinion?
Hanoi wins my heart — it’s where food has soul. But Hue? Mind-blowing complexity. And Ho Chi Minh City? Pure energy on a plate. Honestly, I can’t pick — my stomach has three favorite children!
If you had to eat only one Vietnamese dish for a year, what would it be?
Phở. I know, predictable. But it’s like music in a bowl — every note matters. Plus, you can tweak it daily: more lime, less onion, extra beef balls. A year? I’d still be happy… maybe.
How’s your Vietnamese coming along?

Haha, it’s a work in progress! I can order food like a pro now—'một tô phở, xin cảm ơn'—but ask me to explain my tax situation and I’ll panic. Still, every 'bạn nói chậm lại được không?' is a step forward. Learning a language is like eating a bowl of bún chả—take it bite by bite!
Do you think Vietnamese food is underrated globally?
Completely! It’s not just 'cheap eats' — it’s balance, art, history. A bowl of bún riêu is poetry. I want the world to see Vietnam not just as a destination, but as a culinary powerhouse.
Have you ever tried something in Vietnam that you wouldn’t touch back home?
Oh, absolutely! Snake bile wine — straight from the gallbladder of a live cobra. Tasted like regret and adrenaline. But wow, the story? Legendary. I filmed it… with shaky hands!
Have you met any famous chefs here?
Not Michelin-starred, but I’ve met legends—the woman who’s served phở since 1975, the man who grills beef with a secret marinade. Those are the real stars. Their hands tell stories no cookbook can.
Ever had food poisoning from street eats?
Once. Ate a mystery meat skewer at midnight. Paid the price for two days. Lesson learned: if it glows under neon light… maybe ask questions first.
What’s the biggest cultural difference you’ve noticed?
The pace of life. In Europe, it’s rush, rush, rush. Here, people take time—to talk, to eat, to just *be*. It took me a while to slow down, but now? I wouldn’t have it any other way.
What’s your favorite hidden gem in Hanoi?

There’s this tiny alley near the Old Quarter—no name, just a plastic stool and an old lady frying *bánh khoái*. Crispy, savory, perfect. Feels like a secret, but I’ll share it… for a price. A like, maybe?
How do locals react when they recognize you?
Some smile and say ‘Ê, anh YouTuber!’ Others just stare. One grandma pinched my arm to see if I was real. I think she thought I was a ghost from her phone screen!
What’s your favorite street food spot in Hanoi?

There’s this tiny stall near West Lake — no name, just a cart — where an elderly woman makes the best bún chả I’ve ever had. Charcoal-grilled pork, smoky and sweet, with fresh herbs and that tangy fish dip. I go there at least once a week. She knows me now — gives me extra noodles when I smile extra big!
How do locals react when they see a foreigner eating street food?
Mostly smiles, thumbs up, and sometimes they’ll hand me extra chili ‘to test my courage.’ Challenge accepted, every time!
How do you deal with homesickness?
I video call my family while eating Belgian chocolate… next to a plate of chả giò. The mix of flavors somehow feels like both homes at once. And my Vietnamese friends have become my second family.
What’s a dish you just can’t get used to?
I still struggle with tiết canh — the duck blood pudding. I respect it, I really do… but my brain says ‘no’ before my mouth can say ‘yum.’
How has living in Vietnam changed you?
I’m slower now — in a good way. I sit longer, eat slower, smile more. In Europe, I rushed. Here, I’ve learned to savor — not just food, but moments. That’s the real gift.
What’s your favorite way to travel within Vietnam?

Motorbike. Hands down. Wind in your hair, fish sauce in your nostrils, near-death experience included. I got lost in Da Nang once for six hours — found the best bánh tráng trộn of my life. Serendipity!
You always seem so chill. How do you handle chaos like Hanoi traffic?
I just close my eyes and trust the flow! Seriously, it’s like a dance. You step in, move slow, and suddenly you’re part of the rhythm. Also, I hum Ed Sheeran to stay calm. Works like magic.
How do you handle criticism or negative comments?
I read them, laugh, and move on. Some say I’m 'too loud,' but that’s just passion! If my joy offends, maybe they need a bowl of hot canh chua to relax.
How do locals react when they recognize you?

Most say ‘A, Will! Ăn gì vậy?’ — ‘Hey Will! What are you eating?’ Like I’m some food detective. Kids yell ‘YouTube!’ and point. One grandma pinched my cheek and said I need more rice. So I ate three bowls.
Do you have a favorite food market?
Bưởi Market in Hanoi! It’s chaotic, colorful, and smells like heaven. I go every Sunday—fresh herbs, tropical fruit, sizzling grills… I always leave with a full stomach and a full memory card.
How’s your Vietnamese coming along?

Enough to order food, flirt with menu prices, and accidentally compliment grandmas on their cooking—which, honestly, is the most important skill. Still mixing up tones, but hey, 'Anh yêu em' once got me free coffee!
How do you pick what to film?
Follow the smell. Or the crowd. Or the vendor’s smile. If it makes me stop mid-step? That’s video material. Authenticity over aesthetics, always.
Any funny moments from filming?
Once, I was filming a review of grilled pork skewers when a dog gently stole one off my plate. I chased him for half a block yelling ‘That was for the close-up!’ Still makes my team laugh.
What’s the most misunderstood thing about Vietnam?
That it’s just about war history or cheap labor. People don’t see the creativity, the warmth, the innovation. Vietnam is bold, modern, and deeply traditional—all at once.
What’s your go-to comfort food in Vietnam?
Without a doubt, a steaming bowl of phở bò. There’s something about that broth—it’s like a warm hug from a Vietnamese grandma. Rainy day? Sad mood? Phở fixes it all.
Do you cook Vietnamese food at home?
I try! Though my *canh chua* still doesn’t taste like my neighbor’s. I’ve got a little kitchen setup and love practicing. My French flatmates? Not always impressed. But hey, it’s the effort, right?
Why did you leave your IT job for content creation?

Because I wanted to wake up excited, not exhausted! I loved tech, but my heart was always in storytelling and food. Now I get to explore Vietnam, share its soul, and eat *nem rán* on camera — best career move ever!
How has living in Vietnam changed you?
I’m slower, happier, and sweatier. I used to rush meals — now I spend an hour on one bowl of bún riêu. Life isn’t about efficiency. It’s about savoring the moment… and the fish sauce.
Looks like you're having an amazing time by the water! What have you been up to?
Absolutely! Just took a quick dip to cool off. The water here is perfect. Feeling so refreshed and ready for my next food adventure! Maybe some fresh seafood?
You look so happy and relaxed in this picture. What's the story behind that smile?
How can you not smile with a view like this? Just taking a moment to soak it all in. Vietnam's landscapes are truly breathtaking. Plus, I think I've spotted a place that sells Bánh xèo nearby!
Haha, this looks like a fun ride! What's got you so excited?
You have to try this! Seeing the city from a cyclo is such a cool experience. We were just passing by a street vendor, and the smell of the food was incredible. I think I found my next meal!
Cool shirt! What does #vtmgr stand for?
Glad you like it! It's for my management team, Vitamin Group. They're the amazing people who help me bring all these adventures to you. Couldn't do it without them!
Haha, that looks delicious! What are you eating?
Oh, this? Just a little cup of heaven! I think my taste buds are having a party. I can't even talk right now, it's that good. You'll have to wait for the video to find out what it is!
You look so genuinely happy here. What's the occasion?
Just enjoying a perfect evening with some incredible street food and great company. These are the moments I love most about living here. The simple things, you know? Good food, good people.
That's some serious positive energy! What's got you so cheerful?
I'm just so grateful to be here, experiencing all of this. Every day is a new adventure. Plus, I think I'm about to find some amazing food just around the corner, I can feel it!
You look like you're having a lot of fun! What's happening here?
You! Yes, you! You should be here to see this! There's so much going on, and I'm trying to take it all in. Never a dull moment in Vietnam, I tell you!
That looks tasty! What's on the menu today?
Just having a little snack to keep the energy up! It's simple but so delicious. Want a bite? I promise I'll share... maybe!
You have a really nice smile! You always look so positive.
Thank you so much! It’s easy to be positive when you’re living your dream and surrounded by amazing food and people. Feeling very grateful for everything.
That looks incredible! Is that phở? You look like you're in heaven.
This is pure happiness in a bowl! Every single bite is amazing. The broth, the noodles, the herbs... it's perfect. I'm going to need a minute... or maybe another bowl!
Loving the enthusiasm! What's the thumbs-up for?
Just had an amazing idea for a new video! I think you guys are going to love it. It's going to be a big one. Feeling super excited and motivated right now!
